concepts.title: Nature of Thinking and Mental Imagery

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nature of Thinking and Mental Imagery' refers to.
questions.a: Thinking is the mental manipulation of representations -- concepts, images and symbols -- when the actual object is absent. It needs no immediate stimulus, works through internal symbols, and often borrows mental imagery, as when you picture your route home before setting out.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nature of Thinking and Mental Imagery'.
questions.a: Thinking moves the world inside the head -- absent objects handled as concepts and images.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Reasoning and Problem Solving' refers to.
questions.a: Reasoning draws conclusions from given information -- inductively from cases or deductively from premises. Problem solving runs through steps: identify the problem, represent it, form strategies like means-end analysis or algorithms, apply them and evaluate; mental set and functional fixedness are the classic obstacles.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Reasoning and Problem Solving'.
questions.a: From premises to conclusions, from obstacle to strategy -- problem solving is thinking with a destination.

concepts.title: Decision Making, Judgment and Creative Thinking

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Decision Making, Judgment and Creative Thinking' refers to.
questions.a: Judgment and decision making weigh options under uncertainty, often using shortcuts that can bias us. Creative thinking breaks set: it is novel, useful and fluent, nourished by brainstorming, divergent production and tolerance of unusual ideas -- the opposite of rigid, convergent habit.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Decision Making, Judgment and Creative Thinking'.
questions.a: Decisions use shortcuts; creation breaks them -- fluency, flexibility and originality mark the creative mind.
